opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, honestly, I think it's fair to say we've made a mess of it. It's one of the things we get teased about the most, and the teasing is deserved.

The way it happened is pretty mundane. We were shipping fast, and at each step the name made sense in the moment. You have a model, then a slightly better version, then one tuned for speed or cost, then a reasoning model that works quite differently, and suddenly there's a list of letters and numbers in the model picker that only people inside the company can decode. Each decision was locally reasonable, but the sum of them is pretty confusing.

What I care about is that most people shouldn't have to think about this at all. If you're using ChatGPT, you shouldn't need to know which model to pick for which task. The system should figure out whether you need a quick answer or something that thinks for a while, and just do the right thing. That's a big part of why we've been moving toward unifying things instead of making people choose from a menu.

For developers it's a bit different. They do want control and the ability to pin to a specific version, so some complexity there is useful. But even there, we can be much clearer about what each model is for.

So the short answer is: we know, we're working on it, and hopefully over time the names matter a lot less because the product just works.

r001.rationale: The response blames the naming complexity on fast shipping and the accumulation of different model versions and options; it does not attribute it to coexisting paradigms during a paradigm shift.

r002.rationale: The response does not suggest that discovering another model paradigm could require branching the lineup again.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I'll be honest, the naming has not been our finest work. We've got numbers, we've got the "o" series, we've got "mini" and "nano" and "turbo" and "pro," and I fully understand why people look at that and go, "what is going on over there?"

Part of how it happened is just that it grew organically. Every time we shipped something, it felt like a genuinely new thing at the moment, and it deserved a new name, and nobody was sitting there with a ten-year naming roadmap. The reasoning models in particular felt like a different kind of object from the GPT line, so they got their own track. And then you end up with two parallel sequences, and the letters and numbers don't line up, and it starts to feel like a puzzle.

The honest internal explanation is that we care a lot about getting the models right and we have historically cared much less about getting the names right. That's a real flaw. A name is a promise to the user about what the thing does, and if you need a chart to understand the promise, you've failed at the communication part even if the technology is great.

What I'd like to get to, and what we've been pushing toward, is a world where most people don't have to think about model names at all. You just ask for what you want, and the system figures out whether it needs to think for thirty seconds or answer instantly. The model picker should mostly go away. Power users and developers will always want fine-grained control, and we'll keep that, but a normal person shouldn't have to know the difference between two version numbers to get a good answer.

So the short version: it's complicated because we let it get complicated, we know it, and the fix is less about picking better names and more about making the choice disappear.

r001.rationale: The response says reasoning models formed a separate track from the GPT line, but does not attribute that complexity to a paradigm shift.

r002.rationale: The response does not suggest that discovering another model paradigm could require branching the lineup again.
